text: The CPU-based Horizontal Pod Autoscaler you've already used assumes the resource you care about is CPU, and that a new replica is ready almost immediately. Neither is true for GPU inference. A model server can sit at five percent CPU while its GPU is fully saturated, and spinning up a new GPU-backed pod can mean provisioning a whole new node, pulling a multi-gigabyte image, and loading weights into memory — a process measured in minutes, not seconds.

That combination makes naive autoscaling expensive in both directions: scale too late and you blow your latency budget while capacity is still booting; scale too eagerly with no floor and you pay for GPU nodes sitting mostly idle between bursts. The fix starts with scaling on the right metric — real GPU utilization from the DCGM exporter and Prometheus, read through the Prometheus Adapter as a custom metric the HPA can actually act on.

For workloads with real bursts and long idle gaps, KEDA extends Kubernetes autoscaling down to zero replicas, triggered by something like queue depth instead of a utilization average. The tradeoff is explicit and worth saying out loud: you accept cold-start latency on the first request after idle time, in exchange for paying nothing while genuinely idle. That's the right call for low-frequency bursty traffic, and the wrong one for anything with a tight p99 SLO.

When traffic instead follows a known daily shape — busy during the day, quiet overnight — scale-to-zero's cold start hits right when load resumes. Pre-warming keeps a baseline of replicas ready ahead of that known peak instead, whether through a minReplicas floor on the HPA or a scheduled scaler that raises the floor before the surge arrives, so the capacity is already warm when it's actually needed.

None of this works if pod-level and node-level autoscaling disagree. HPA or KEDA decide how many pods you want; the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter decide whether a GPU node exists to run them on. Add replicas faster than nodes can be provisioned and pods just sit Pending. Tuning both together, and sharing GPUs across small pods with time-slicing or MIG, is what makes any of these autoscaling patterns deliver the capacity they promise.
